design_detail: Narrative review by three forensic medicine authors (Monash University and the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine) of published case reports of cardiovascular presentations to hospital temporally linked to cannabis (31 reports, 35 people; Table 1), of published deaths linked to cannabis (6 publications, 13 men; Table 2) and of 12 epidemiological studies of cannabis use and cardiovascular disease (Table 3), with background on THC and CBD pharmacology and a discussion of when a death should be attributed to cannabis in death investigation. Search in PubMed and Scopus with listed keywords, English only, plus reference-chasing; no dates, counts, screening or appraisal reported; synthesis limited to counts and medians from the case tables. Synthetic cannabinoids were excluded.
can_establish: That published case reports describe cardiovascular emergencies and 13 deaths shortly after cannabis use, many in men with coronary disease, which epidemiological studies existed by early 2019, and how three forensic medicine authors proposed that deaths be attributed to cannabis.
cannot_establish: Whether cannabis caused any of the deaths described, how often cannabis contributes to sudden cardiac death in the population, or whether deaths involving cannabis are under- or over-counted: the case reports have no comparison or denominator and are not appraised, and the review gives no data on how often THC is present in sudden deaths not attributed to it.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). English-language publications found in PubMed and Scopus with keywords (marijuana or cannabis with fatality, death, poisoning, arrhythmias, heart, myocardial infarction) and by following citations (p. 299, §2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: publications in which cannabis was believed to have contributed to an emergency admission for a cardiovascular or related event, or to have contributed to or caused a death; epidemiological studies designed to examine a link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease. Excluded: synthetic cannabinoids; non-English publications (p. 299, §2). The tables are titled as summaries of selected publications, and Table 1 summarizes 31 of what the text calls numerous reports, without saying how they were chosen (pp. 300–301).
sample.demographics: Hospital reports: 35 people aged 15–53, 5 of them women (p. 301). Deaths: 13 men aged 17–52 (p. 301; Table 2, p. 302).
sample.selection_effects: Published case reports are chosen by their authors for a suspected link; deaths in which cannabis was present but judged irrelevant are not published, so the reports cannot show how often a link is real or how often THC is found in sudden deaths generally. The review's case set is smaller than that of a systematic review it cites (81 case reports with 116 people; p. 302). The 9 deaths among French addictovigilance notifications in Table 3 (p. 303) are not added to the count of 13.

exposure.measurement: In the case reports, cannabis use comes from history, urine cannabinoid screens or, in 8 of the 13 deaths, THC measured in blood; specimen site and interval from death to sampling are not given (Tables 1–2, pp. 300–302). In the epidemiological studies, use is mostly self-reported or taken from hospital coding, with urine testing in a few (Table 3, p. 303).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Mostly smoked cannabis in the case reports, with frequency and timing recorded unevenly; not used on this card.
exposure.polysubstance: The text says other drugs were excluded as far as possible by history or testing and that none were implicated (pp. 301–302), but the tables record alcohol, sildenafil, LSD, tobacco and, in one hospital case, a synthetic cannabinoid in the past week, and alcohol in two of the deaths (blood alcohol 0.04% and 0.119%) (pp. 300–302).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Time since last use is given in some case reports (from minutes to the previous evening) and unknown in others; for the deaths, the interval from death to post-mortem sampling is not reported.

comparison.controls: None for the case reports. The epidemiological studies used their own comparisons (control periods in a case-crossover design, people not using cannabis in cohorts and hospital databases), as summarized in Table 3 (p. 303).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: In the case reports, pre-existing coronary disease (significant atherosclerosis or other pathology in 8 of the 13 deaths), channelopathies, tobacco smoking and other risk factors are recorded unevenly and not weighed case by case.

outcomes.instruments: Hospital presentations: acute myocardial infarction confirmed by creatine kinase or troponin, arrhythmias, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, Brugada pattern, myocarditis. Deaths: autopsy findings where an autopsy was done, and the cause of death as given by the case authors or, in one case, a coroner.
outcomes.validity_norms: No causality assessment is applied to the case reports, and the review's own criteria for attributing a death to a drug (below) are not applied to the 13 deaths it counts.
outcomes.operationalization: A cannabis-associated death is a published death that the case authors (or a coroner) linked to recent cannabis use, with or without THC measured in blood.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooling. From the case tables: 35 people with hospital presentations (median age printed 25), 24 without evidence of coronary artery disease, 18 with confirmed acute myocardial infarction; 13 deaths, blood THC 1.9–22 ng/mL in 8. Relayed from Table 3 (p. 303): AMI risk 4.8 (95% CI 2.9–9.5) in the hour after smoking cannabis and 1.7 (0.6–5.1) in the second hour (Mittleman et al., case-crossover); after MI, mortality hazard 4.2 (1.2–14) for weekly use and 2.5 (0.9–7.3) for less than weekly use (Mukamal et al.); 29% higher long-term mortality, not significant (Frost et al.); acute ischaemic stroke adjusted RR 1.17 (1.15–1.20) (Rumalla et al.); cardiovascular mortality adjusted HR 2.22 (printed as 90% CI 1.27–3.70) in young adults with MI (DeFilippis et al.); no association of lifetime or recent use with cardiovascular mortality in CARDIA (Reis et al.).
analysis.selective_reporting: Selection among the case reports is not explained; the French notification series' 9 deaths are not counted; the text's summaries of the case tables and of Table 3 differ from the tables in several places (see reporting issues).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Thirty-one case reports describe 35 people with cardiovascular emergencies during or soon after cannabis use, and six publications describe 13 men aged 17–52 whose deaths their authors linked to recent cannabis use. Of the 13, 8 had significant coronary atherosclerosis or other pathology; THC was measured in blood in 8 (1.9–22 ng/mL), the other 5 resting on urine cannabinoids or history, one with no THC found in blood; alcohol was present in 2; two died days after admission and one had no autopsy. Of 12 epidemiological studies tabulated, several report associations with myocardial infarction or stroke, one long cohort found no association with cardiovascular mortality, and two systematic reviews disagree. The authors themselves write that the evidence for a link with increased risk of cardiovascular death is not clear and the risk probably rare (p. 304).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says at least 13 deaths from a cardiovascular mechanism have been reported from use of the drug, and that this is “very likely to be an under-estimate” (p. 298), but presents no data on under-ascertainment. It recommends that, with very recent use, a positive blood THC and a possible cardiac or cerebrovascular cause, cannabis should be considered at least a contributory cause of sudden or unexpected death (p. 298), and the conclusion says inclusion of cannabis as cause or contributor “in appropriate cases is to be encouraged” (p. 304). These recommendations rest on case reports without comparison groups, in which coronary disease and alcohol were often present; 5 of the 13 deaths counted would fail the review's own requirement of a blood THC test (p. 304); its general rule that a drug must be present at a concentration capable of causing death cannot be applied to THC, for which the authors say no minimum concentration can be given (p. 304), so attribution would rest on THC being present plus circumstances. Post-mortem changes in THC concentration are not discussed. Applied in certification, the recommendation would raise counts of deaths attributed to cannabis without evidence on how often THC is present in sudden cardiac deaths that cannabis did not cause.

timeline.event: Bachs and Mørland: six deaths of men aged 17–43 attributed to cannabis, blood THC 2–22 ng/mL, most with coronary artery disease (as summarized in Table 2, p. 302).

Mittleman et al., case-crossover in 3882 people with acute MI: risk 4.8 times baseline in the hour after smoking cannabis (as summarized, pp. 302–303); the AHA 2020 statement, as recorded on its card, relays this estimate as resting on 9 people who had used cannabis within an hour of presenting with AMI.

Tormey: a coroner's court case with no THC in blood in which cannabis was found a secondary cause of death, and a discussion advising that cannabis be considered contributory only with use within 2 h of the arrest and ideally with blood THC confirmed (as summarized, pp. 302, 304).
Hartung et al.: two sudden deaths of young men with blood THC 5.2 and 1.9 ng/mL (as summarized in Table 2, p. 302); on the deaths reading list to be read with this review.

Jouanjus et al., systematic review (81 case reports, 29 observational studies): association with cardiovascular disease, stronger for ischaemic stroke; Reis et al. (CARDIA, 5113 young adults, over 25 years): no association with cardiovascular mortality (as summarized, pp. 302–303).
Ravi et al., systematic review: no compelling evidence linking cannabis use with mortality, including from AMI (as summarized, p. 302).
AHA scientific statement on cannabis and cardiovascular health: the evidence on adverse cardiovascular outcomes is still inconclusive (as recorded on its card).
Rock et al., characteristics of deaths following cannabis use in England, 1998–2020: on the deaths reading list, not yet read.

replication.where_it_stands: Case reports show that sudden cardiovascular deaths shortly after cannabis use have been attributed to cannabis by case authors and coroners. Whether recent cannabis use raises the risk of sudden cardiac death has not been measured in any controlled study read here; the cohort and review evidence summarized in this paper, and the AHA 2020 statement, call it unclear or inconclusive. The paper is cited mainly as the forensic argument for counting cannabis as a contributory cause, and its recommendation should be shown with that evidence base.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement. The Declaration covers only originality and approval by the authors (p. 305).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: no conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Department of Forensic Medicine, Monash University, and the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine, that is, from the death-investigation setting whose certification practice the review addresses; the acknowledgments thank the Institute, the Department and Professor Stephen Cordner (p. 305). Received 28 November 2018, accepted 7 March 2019.

what_would_settle_it: A population-based study of sudden cardiac deaths with complete toxicology (blood THC with the interval from death to sampling) compared with suitable controls, such as deaths from external causes or living people from the same population, with coronary disease, tobacco and alcohol measured, to estimate whether recent cannabis use raises the risk of sudden cardiac death and how often THC is present in such deaths without having contributed.

domains.note: Databases and keywords are named, but no dates, counts, screening or flow; the tables are explicitly selections, and the case set is smaller than that of a systematic review the authors cite.

The case reports on which the conclusions rest are not appraised for causality or alternative causes; Table 3 has a comments column listing limitations of the epidemiological studies, but the text's summary does not use it.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The cases and epidemiological studies are by others; the authors' own work is cited only for background on driving.
The discussion hedges (arguably, conceivably, at least in theory), but the abstract states 13 deaths from use of the drug and an under-estimate without data.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against cannabis as a cause of cardiovascular death
domains.note: The text counts 11 of 12 epidemiological studies as showing increased risk, although Table 3 includes a null cohort and a study finding less atherosclerosis; coronary disease, alcohol and tobacco in the fatal cases are not weighed; the denominator (THC in deaths not attributed to cannabis) is not considered.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The search and selection are undocumented, the case reports are not appraised, and the text's summaries of its own tables lean towards a causal reading. The discussion is more cautious than the abstract. Citable for: what the published case reports describe (counts, ages, findings, toxicology, as in Tables 1–2); the epidemiological estimates as relayed, pointing to the primary studies; the authors' proposed criteria and recommendations for attributing death to cannabis, presented as their position; their statement that no minimum post-mortem THC concentration can indicate cause. Not citable for: cannabis having caused any of these deaths; the size of any cardiovascular risk; undercounting of cannabis-related deaths.

key_findings.finding: Methods: English-language publications on deaths attributed to cannabis (synthetic cannabinoids excluded) were searched in PubMed and Scopus with keywords and by following citations; included were reports in which cannabis was believed to have contributed to an emergency admission for a cardiovascular or related event or to a death, and epidemiological studies designed to examine a link with cardiovascular disease. No search dates, numbers screened or appraisal method are given.

Hospital presentations (Table 1): Thirty-one case reports describe 35 people aged 15–53 (median printed as 25), 5 of them women; cannabis use was not always confirmed by testing and, when tested, usually by urine cannabinoids; most had chest pain, arrhythmia or coronary thrombus; 24 had no evidence of coronary artery disease and 18 had acute myocardial infarction confirmed by creatine kinase or troponin; there were 5 strokes or transient ischaemic attacks secondary to a cardiovascular event, 3 possible Brugada syndromes and 1 myocarditis.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 1: median age 26 overall and 35 for the five women (printed 33).

key_findings.finding: Deaths (Table 2): six publications describe 13 men aged 17–52 (median 37) whose deaths their authors linked to recent cannabis use; in eight there was significant coronary atherosclerosis and/or other pathology (three with superimposed thrombus, two with enlarged hearts, at least three diagnosed with AMI); five are described as having little obvious pathology (aged 17–42, mean 31).

Toxicology of the thirteen deaths as tabulated: THC in blood in 8 (Bachs and Mørland's six men: 22, 4, 2, 5, 3 and 7 ng/mL; Hartung et al.'s two: 5.2 and 1.9 ng/mL); the other five rested on urine cannabinoids (Tormey; Casier et al., two cases; Orsini et al.) or history with urine confirmation (Dines et al.). In Tormey's case no THC was found in blood, yet the coroner found cannabis a secondary cause of death. Blood alcohol was 0.04% in one of Bachs and Mørland's cases and 0.119% in Orsini et al.'s; one of Casier et al.'s cases had a history of alcohol problems.
key_findings.note: The text (§6, 5th paragraph) summarizes this as 8 blood-positive (2–22 ng/mL, median 4), 4 urine-positive and 1 with no cannabinoid measurement; see reporting issues. Editors' calculation from Table 2: median of the 8 blood values 4.5 ng/mL.

key_findings.finding: Circumstances of the thirteen deaths (Table 2): two of Casier et al.'s cases died days after admission (fatal ventricular tachycardia 3 days later; multiple organ failure a few days later); Dines et al.'s case had no autopsy, with rhythm disturbance only possible; one of Bachs and Mørland's cases had a previous MI and widespread coronary disease; Orsini et al.'s case had an extensive MI with hypertensive and atherosclerotic heart disease.

Epidemiological studies as relayed (Table 3): case-crossover study of 3882 people with acute MI (1258 women), risk 4.8 (95% CI 2.9–9.5) within 1 h of smoking cannabis and 1.7 (0.6–5.1) within 2 h, without toxicology; cohort of 1913 people after MI, mortality HR 4.2 (1.2–14) for weekly use and 2.5 (0.9–7.3) for less than weekly use; 3886 people followed 18 years (519 deaths, 22 reporting cannabis use), mortality 29% higher, not significant; national inpatient data, acute ischaemic stroke adjusted RR 1.17 (1.15–1.20); 2097 people with MI before age 51, cannabis use in 6.0%, cardiovascular mortality adjusted HR 2.22 (printed 90%CI 1.27–3.70); CARDIA, 5113 young adults followed over 25 years (84% reported cannabis use), no association with cardiovascular mortality; French addictovigilance 2006–10, 35 (1.8%) cannabis-related notifications cardiovascular, 9 deaths.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows Mittleman, Mukamal, Frost, Rumalla, DeFilippis, Reis, Jouanjus
key_findings.note: Second-hand estimates; cite the primary studies. The AHA 2020 statement (card sc_page_2020) relays the 2.22 hazard ratio as for people who used cocaine and marijuana, without saying whether the exposures were combined.

key_findings.finding: The authors say eleven of the twelve epidemiological studies showed trends to increased mortality or significant associations with increased risk; they also summarize two systematic reviews that disagree: one (81 case reports with 116 people, 29 observational studies, 3 clinical trials, 2 experimental studies) found an association with cardiovascular disease, stronger for ischaemic stroke; the other found no compelling evidence linking cannabis with any mortality, including from AMI.
key_findings.note: The count of 11 does not match Table 3 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: In the Discussion the authors state that the larger retrospective studies and systematic reviews leave the link between cannabis use and increased risk of cardiovascular death unclear; that the symptoms and diseases described may have other causes (rhythm disturbance, undiagnosed channelopathies, tobacco smoking); that a small number of susceptible people with other morbidities could still be harmed; and that the risk is probably rare.

Proposed criteria for attributing death to a drug: with no clear evidence from the scene, pathologists should exclude other reasonable explanations and establish that the drug can cause death by an understood mechanism, is present at a concentration capable of doing so, and fits the circumstances. For THC, the authors say no minimum blood concentration can be given that might indicate cause, because of delays from death to sampling; most laboratories detect 1–2 ng/mL in post-mortem blood, and they suggest lower values may reflect use days earlier; if THC is quantified and the case fits the criteria, they argue this could suffice to list cannabis as causal or contributory. They require a blood THC test, not urine cannabinoids or history alone, to link a death to recent use, and cite Tormey's advice that cannabis be considered contributory only with use within 2 h of the arrest, ideally with blood THC confirmed.

Counting recommendations: the authors write that, ideally, the presence of cannabis (as THC) should be recorded in death statistics so as not to underestimate cannabis-associated mortality, and conclude that including cannabis as a cause or contributor in appropriate cases is to be encouraged so that global burden of disease estimates reflect its harm; the abstract adds that the 13 reported deaths are very likely an under-estimate.

Background stated in the review (citing earlier pharmacokinetic studies): after smoking, blood THC falls below 10% of its peak within an hour and below 5 ng/mL within a few hours; oral use gives lower peak THC concentrations, usually under 5 ng/mL, with an active metabolite (11-hydroxy-THC) formed in larger amounts.

The review also mentions, without detail, well over 50 published reports of arteritis with long-term heavy cannabis use, many leading to limb amputation, and deaths attributed to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (four references).

reporting_issues.issue: Ages in Table 1 give a median of 26 for the 35 people and 35 for the five women (24, 33, 35, 36, 45); the text prints 25 and 33 (editors' calculation; the one age given as 40s lies above the median and does not affect it).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite ages from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The 28-year-old in Hartung et al.'s report is described with histological signs of single-cell necrosis in the heart in Table 2 and on p. 301, but on p. 302 as having no histopathological evidence of cellular necrosis.
reporting_issues.consequence: Contradiction about the one death the review presents as an acute ischaemic event without structural heart disease.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 8 deaths had THC in blood (2–22 ng/mL, median 4), 4 had urine cannabinoids and 1 had no cannabinoid measurement (p. 302). Table 2 shows 8 blood values of 1.9–22 ng/mL (median 4.5, editors' calculation) and 5 cases confirmed only by urine, one of them (Tormey) with no THC found in blood, and no case without any cannabinoid test.
reporting_issues.consequence: Five of the 13 deaths lack blood THC confirmation, which the review itself requires to link a death to recent use (p. 304); one had a negative blood THC.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says no other drugs were implicated in the hospital cases or the deaths (pp. 301–302), and the Methods exclude synthetic cannabinoids (p. 299), but the tables record alcohol in two deaths (blood alcohol 0.04% and 0.119%) and a history of alcohol problems in a third, and among hospital cases heavy alcohol use, alcohol with cannabis, sildenafil 36 h earlier, LSD 2 days earlier and a synthetic cannabinoid within the past week (Table 1, cases 6, 12, 16, 26, 29).
reporting_issues.consequence: Co-exposures were present and not weighed; the case set includes one exposure the Methods say was excluded.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 11 of the 12 epidemiological studies showed trends to increased mortality or significant associations with increased risk (p. 302), but in Table 3 Reis et al. (CARDIA) found no association with cardiovascular mortality, Lee et al. found less angiographic atherosclerosis in people who used cannabis, and Jouanjus et al. and Dines et al. are descriptive series without a comparison group (p. 303). The text also lists Frost et al. among studies that found an increased risk (p. 302), while Table 3 reports its 29% excess as not significant.
reporting_issues.consequence: The count overstates the epidemiological support; by the editors' reading of Table 3, at most 8 rows report a raised risk estimate, some of them non-significant.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 prints the Petronis and Anthony interval as 95% CI 1555–3.25 and the DeFilippis et al. interval as a 90% CI; the Mittleman et al. interval (4.8, 95% CI 2.9–9.5) is not symmetric around the estimate on the log scale (editors' check).
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one misprint and possibly more; take intervals from the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: The five deaths with little obvious pathology (mean age printed as 31) cannot be identified unambiguously: the five described by their findings match Table 2 cases aged 40, 42, 17, 28 and 37 (mean 32.8, editors' calculation), and the epilepsy case said to be one of them (Dines et al., 18) had no autopsy. The phrase “little or obvious pathology” appears to omit a word.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the group of deaths without significant heart disease is not clearly defined.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that relatively few deaths are attributed to cannabis itself cites four reports of deaths from synthetic cannabinoids (refs. 23, 24, 26, 27).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor citation error; the statement has no supporting reference.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Forensic Sci Int 298:298–306, pp. 298–306 (all pages including the reference list; Tables 1–3 and every number on this card checked on rendered pages; no supplement; no funding or conflict statement in the article).
